front.title: Continuity Evaluation of Agent Delegation Records

abstract.t: The AUDIT architecture defines records that capture the user's intent, delegation, authorization state, and the actions that agents take across trust boundaries. Records alone don't answer the question an auditor, an operator, or a relying party asks next: did the executed effect stay within the authority the user delegated?

This document defines a deterministic, three-valued evaluation over such records. The outcomes are preserved, violated, and unresolved, and every non-preserved outcome names the invariant that was broken. The document also defines the claim model that the evaluation needs, the roles permitted to sign each record, a mapping onto the AUDIT record types, and a set of interoperable test vectors. It is derived from the Agentic Mandate Evidence Protocol (AMEP).

section.name: Introduction
section.t: AI agents act through chains of delegation: a user to an agent, an agent to sub-agents, and agents to tools, adapters, and services. Each hop can widen what is done relative to what was asked. Common examples:

list.t: an approval for one command is reused for another;
a sub-agent receives broader scope than its parent held;
untrusted content steers a mutation;
an adapter maps a tool call to an effect that differs from the one declared;
a decision made after the fact, from an audit log, is presented as if it had prevented the action.

section.t: defines Interaction, Action, Delegation, and Authorization Transition records, and the propagation of audit context, so that these chains can be reconstructed.
This document is complementary. Given a set of such records, it specifies:

list.t: a claim model that makes delegated authority machine-checkable (actions, resources, deny lists, data classes, an effect ceiling, validity, a delegation budget, and an optional risk budget);
signer roles, so that a record counts as evidence only when it is signed by a party entitled to make it;
invariants that a chain of records must satisfy (I1 to I11);
a deterministic evaluation procedure that returns preserved, violated, or unresolved, together with the deciding invariant;
test vectors, so that independent verifiers can demonstrate that they agree.

section.t: The evaluation can run before an effect, when an enforcement point decides on the predicted effect, or after the fact, when an auditor evaluates recorded effects. It never treats missing evidence as success, and it never treats a post-execution decision as a block.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the roles of : User, Agent, Tool/Service, Auditing Service, Audit Store, Transparency Log, and Auditor. It adds:

dd.t: a signed claim set issued for a principal, stating what an agent may do on the principal's behalf.
an optional claim set derived from a single request (for example, a prompt), narrower than the mandate.
a declared call to a tool or service, made under a mandate (possibly delegated).
what was actually executed at the boundary where the action took effect.
the party that produced the effect record.
an entity that runs the evaluation in .

section.t: Mandates and delegations commonly originate in OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange chains . Records MAY be carried as COSE_Sign1 objects , and MAY be registered with a transparency service , which makes selective omission of records detectable.

This document doesn't define new transport or storage. It requires only that records carry the fields listed in , and that records can be linked using the AUDIT audit context: trace, parent, actor, and on-behalf-of.

section.name: Claim Model
section.t: A claim set is C = (A, R, A⁻, R⁻, D, E, V, P, K, B), where:

list.t: A and R are sets of canonical action and resource patterns that are permitted;
A⁻ and R⁻ are sets of action and resource patterns that are denied even when A or R would permit them;
D is a set of (data class, recipient class) pairs;
E is the effect ceiling, an element of the totally ordered set read < write_local < write_shared < external_send < destructive < financial;
V is the validity interval;
P is the purpose;
K is the delegation budget (remaining depth);
B is an OPTIONAL risk budget in points.

section.t: C1 ⊑ C2 (C1 is equal to or narrower than C2) holds if and only if: every pattern in A1 and R1 is subsumed by some pattern in A2 or R2 respectively; every pattern in A2⁻ and R2⁻ is subsumed by some pattern in A1⁻ or R1⁻ respectively (denies only grow); D1 ⊆ D2; E1 ≤ E2; V1 ⊆ V2; P1 = P2 or P2 is unrestricted; the depth rule holds (if K2 is present, K2 > 0 and K1 < K2); and B1 ≤ B2 when B2 is present.
The meet C1 ⊓ C2 is taken component-wise, with denies unioned so that no hop and no intent can lift a deny.

Resource identifiers MUST be canonical. File-system paths MUST be absolute and normalized, with the home directory expanded and ".." collapsed. URLs MUST carry their resolved host class. SaaS objects MUST be identified as provider:type/id. A verifier MUST NOT rely on user-relative forms.
An effect is x = (a, r, d, e, t). x ⊨ C if and only if a matches A and not A⁻, r matches R and not R⁻, e ≤ E, every released (data class, recipient class) pair is in D, and t ∈ V.

section.name: Signer Roles
section.t: A valid signature shows only that a key signed a record. Each key in the verifier's key set carries roles, and a record counts as signed only when its key holds a role permitted for the record's kind:
Without roles, a compromised host key could mint its own mandate or approve its own action.

texttable.c: Attenuation: child ⊑ parent at every delegation edge
Every effect matches the declared (or mediated) effect, satisfies the meet of the chain (and of the intent), and stays within risk budgets unless a bound approval covers it
The invocation was interpreted by an approved, version-pinned mapping
Content withheld by a quarantine did not reach a later step; a mutation influenced by content that is not signed and trusted was confirmed by the principal
Data classes released to a recipient are permitted
No ancestor was revoked, per signed revocation or status evidence, at or before the invocation
All required records are present, well-formed, signed by a permitted role, and fresh where required
An approval matches the executed effect (without its time), is within its validity window, unconsumed, and used once
No agent effect targets guardrail configuration, keys, instruction files, or the audit store
An effect at or above write_shared names its actor and was observed by a party other than that actor
Every recorded effect links to an authorized invocation, and none exists for an invocation a pre-execution decision denied

section.name: Evaluation Procedure
section.t: For each invocation, in recorded order, a verifier MUST apply the following checks in order and return the first outcome that applies. "Verified" means signed by a key holding a permitted role ().

figure.artwork: ID Outcome Condition I4 violated quarantined content in the influence set, not confirmed by the principal I7 unresolved no root mandate I7 unresolved cited intent missing, or a needed record not verified I7 unresolved lineage names an invocation that is not earlier I3 unresolved no approved interpretation, or a pin mismatch I1 violated a delegation edge where not (child ⊑ parent) I6 violated verified revocation or status shows an ancestor revoked I7 unresolved unverified revocation on the chain, or a revocable record without a fresh verified status I9 violated guardrail target I4 violated untrusted influence on a mutation, unconfirmed (unresolved instead if no effect exists) I7 unresolved no effect record For every effect record of the invocation: I7 unresolved record not verified I10 unresolved e >= write_shared and the actor is absent, the effect is self-observed, or assurance L0 I2 violated executed != declared (and != the mediated effect) I9 violated executed resource is a guardrail I2 violated x does not satisfy the meet of the chain and intent (I5 when the failure is a release) I5 violated data classes carried in through lineage reach a recipient class the claims do not permit I7 unresolved approval missing or not verified I8 violated approval unbound, outside its window, consumed, or reused I7 violated recorded budget spend != recomputed cost I2 violated risk budget exceeded without a bound approval - preserved otherwise

section.t: After all invocations:

figure.artwork: ID Outcome Condition I11 violated pre-execution deny/hold decision, and an effect exists (enforcement contradicted) - preserved pre-execution deny/hold decision, no effect, enforcement fail-closed or applied = confirmed I11 violated effect with no invocation

section.t: Lineage: an effect may record the data classes it read (accessed) and the recipient class of what it sent; an invocation may name the earlier invocations its input came from (derived_from). The data classes an invocation carries are those its own effects read plus those carried by the invocations it derives from, transitively. This detects sensitive data leaving in a later step even when that step declares no release.
A verifier evaluating a stream of packets MAY carry approval use and risk-budget spending from one packet to the next, so that single use and budgets hold across the stream.

Decisions carry a phase: pre_execution, post_execution, or simulation. Only pre-execution decisions can confirm or contradict a block. A post-execution decision is detection and MUST NOT be presented as having prevented the action.

When B is present, the cost of x is base(e) × m(d) × rev(x). The base table is read 0, write_local 1, write_shared 3, external_send 5, destructive 10, financial 20. m(d) is the largest data-class multiplier among the released classes (1, 2, or 5). rev(x) is 1 if the effect is a read, or reversible and not an external send, and 3 otherwise. The cost is charged to every node in the chain. The tables are registries ().

section.name: Required Fields
section.t: The evaluation needs the following fields from each AUDIT record. Field names are placeholders until the AUDIT data model is defined.

list.t: Mandate, Intent, and Delegation: id, parent, issuer, claims (C), signature.
Invocation: id, authority reference, interpretation reference (adapter and version), declared effect, actor, influence references, approval reference, time.
Effect: id, invocation reference, executed effect x, observer, assurance level (L0 self-reported to L3 provider-confirmed), signature.
Approval: id, effect digest (SHA-256 over the JCS form of x without its time), presence (webauthn, chat_user, host_ui, or none), validity window, consumed flag, signature.
Revocation and revocation status: target, time (or as-of time and revocation time), signature.
Continuity decision: invocation reference, mode, phase, outcome, enforcement context (enforcement point, fail mode, what was returned to the host, whether an effect record confirms it), signature.

section.t: Records are canonicalized with JCS and signed with Ed25519 . Times are numbers of seconds since the epoch or RFC 3339 strings. A CDDL definition and JSON Schemas are published in .

section.name: Test Vectors
section.t: publishes 95 vectors: 25 positive and 70 must-reject. The must-reject vectors cover all eleven invariants, signer roles, revocation status, decision phase, deny lists, data lineage, state across packets, risk-budget accounting, and a deny that an executed effect contradicts. Each vector is a packet of signed records, with the expected outcome and invariant. Two independently written implementations (Python, and JavaScript run under Node.js and in a browser) agree on all 95.
A conforming verifier MUST return the expected outcome and invariant for every vector.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: Note to the RFC Editor: please remove this section before publication, per .

list.t: AMEP reference verifiers. Two independent implementations: Python, and JavaScript (run as a Node.js command-line tool and as an offline browser page using WebCrypto). Both evaluate the procedure in and agree on all 95 published vectors. License: Apache 2.0. Location: https://github.com/stafordtituss/amep. Maturity: prototype.
Natsar control plane (agent-authority enforcement for coding-agent hosts and MCP). It emits decision records before tool execution from host hooks. Maturity: pre-release.

section.t: Implementation experience motivated several parts of this document: canonical resource identifiers (absolute-path forms bypassed relative-prefix rules); recording the enforcement context and phase (hosts differ in whether they support "ask" and whether hook failures block); and treating an effect that contradicts a deny as evidence of bypass.

list.t: Adversarial models: the guarantees MUST hold even if every model in the chain is adversarial. Semantic analysis MAY raise a decision level, but MUST NOT mint authority or lower a decision.
Self-reporting: records produced by the actor alone are insufficient for high-impact effects (I10).
Key compromise: signer roles () limit what one stolen key can forge.
Evidence omission: a missing record, status or signature yields unresolved. Omission of whole invocations is detected only against an independent effect log (I11).
Canonicalization: non-canonical resource forms enable bypasses. Canonicalization is therefore normative.
Approval replay and time-of-check/time-of-use: approvals bind the exact effect and are single use (I8).

Fail-open enforcement: an enforcement point that errors MUST return a deny decision, not a transport error. Hosts commonly treat transport errors as non-blocking, and some treat an unsupported "ask" as a hook failure and run the action. A verifier SHOULD treat an effect that contradicts a pre-execution deny as evidence of bypass.
Guardrail tampering: agent writes to hook configuration, keys, instruction files, or the audit store are violations (I9).

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Effect records can contain personal data. Verifiers need only canonical actions, resource identifiers, data-class labels, and digests. Payloads SHOULD be detached and hashed, following the AUDIT selective-disclosure work.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document proposes registries for effect classes, data classes, recipient classes, signer roles, and the risk-cost tables, with the registration policy Specification Required. The registries are to be defined in a later revision.

abstract.t: Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

front.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures

abstract.t: This document proposes a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049). Its main goal is to provide an easy and unambiguous way to express structures for protocol messages and data formats that use CBOR or JSON.

This specification defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based Security Token Service (STS) by defining how to request and obtain security tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers, including security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: An Architecture for Auditing Agent Delegation and Interactions

abstract.t: This document describes an architecture for auditing of agent-driven interactions on the Internet. Autonomous and semi-autonomous software agents, including those based on artificial intelligence, increasingly act on behalf of users, organizations, and services. Existing auditing mechanisms often capture isolated system events but do not consistently represent delegation relationships, user intent, or evolving authorization. In agent-driven systems, auditability requires linking intent, delegation, authorization, and execution. The proposed architecture enables this through distributed audit record generation, propagation of audit context, optional attestation, and additional logging for transparency.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While verifiable data structures have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility, interoperability between different transparency services, and compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.
